Environmental values inside points, buffers, tracks and areas

Source: vignettes/workflow-values-in-shapes.Rmd
workflow-values-in-shapes.Rmd

This article shows how to get environmental values inside 3D shapes, such as tag detections, buffers around them, a tag’s track, or a protected area down to a set depth. Each example uses the same three steps:

  1. Build the shapes with as_vector3d(), buffer_3d() or sample_3d().
  2. Intersect each shape with the data: crop() the dataset to the shape, read its time steps with as_voxel(), and keep the values inside the shape with mask().
  3. Summarise the values with summarise_3d().

You loop over the shapes yourself, so you can stop after any step and look at the result. Each example ends with a table of values per shape, which you can join back to your observations. Volumes are in km³ throughout.

Example data

The examples use a small synthetic temperature dataset: a 0.05° grid off eastern Australia, six depth levels from 0 to 200 m, and five daily time steps. Temperature falls with depth, rises to the north and warms a little each day. The code below writes it to a netCDF file, as you might download from Copernicus Marine.

library(ocean3d)

lon <- seq(150.025, 150.975, by = 0.05)
lat <- seq(-20.975, -20.025, by = 0.05)
depth <- c(0, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200)
time <- 0:4
grid <- expand.grid(lon = lon, lat = lat, depth = depth, time = time)
temp <- 28 - 0.06 * grid$depth + 2 * (grid$lat + 20.5) + 0.2 * grid$time

dims <- list(
  ncdf4::ncdim_def("lon", "degrees_east", lon),
  ncdf4::ncdim_def("lat", "degrees_north", lat),
  ncdf4::ncdim_def("depth", "m", depth),
  ncdf4::ncdim_def("time", "days since 2020-03-01", time)
)
var <- ncdf4::ncvar_def("temp", "degC", dims, missval = -9999,
                        prec = "double")
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".nc")
nc <- ncdf4::nc_create(path, var)
ncdf4::ncvar_put(nc, var, array(temp, lengths(lapply(dims, `[[`, "vals"))))
ncdf4::nc_close(nc)

as_proxy() describes the file without reading its values. Each later step reads only the cells and time steps it needs, at every depth level.

proxy <- as_proxy(path)
proxy
#> class      : SpatProxy (experimental)
#> source     : file23945f5151ee.nc
#> variable   : temp (degC)
#> dimensions : 20 x 20 x 6 x 5 (lon x lat x depth x time)
#> lon        : 150.025 to 150.975, 20 cells, edges inferred
#> lat        : -20.975 to -20.025, 20 cells, edges inferred
#> depth      : 0 to 200 m, 6 levels, shallow first, edges inferred
#> time       : 2020-03-01 to 2020-03-05, 5 steps, standard calendar, no bounds
#> crs        : EPSG:4326

Points: tag detections

Three detections, each with a position, a depth and a date, become SpatVector3D points:

obs <- data.frame(
  tag = c("A", "B", "C"),
  lon = c(150.21, 150.52, 150.80),
  lat = c(-20.31, -20.56, -20.82),
  depth = c(12, 48, 140),
  date = as.Date(c("2020-03-01", "2020-03-02", "2020-03-04"))
)
detections <- as_vector3d(obs, time = "date", id = "tag")
detections
#> class      : SpatVector3D
#> geometry   : points 
#> features   : 3 
#> vertices   : 3 
#> depth (m)  : 12 to 140 
#> time       : 2020-03-01 to 2020-03-04

For one detection, crop() keeps the grid cell it falls in, and as_voxel() reads the time step nearest its date. With a shape as time, as_voxel() always returns a list, here with one voxel. mask() then keeps the value at the depth level nearest the detection’s depth, skipping levels without a value:

a <- detections[1]
v <- as_voxel(crop(proxy, a), time = a)[[1]]
summarise_3d(mask(v, a), statistic = "mean")
#>         time  mean n
#> 1 2020-03-01 27.75 1

Detection A at 12 m takes the 10 m level. extract_to_point() gives the same value from the file:

extract_to_point(obs[1, ], path, var = "temp", date_col = "date",
                 method = "nearest")$temp
#> [1] 27.75

Both pick the nearest time step: on this data they give the same values for all three detections, for a time halfway between two steps, and for a date after the last step. Neither warns when the step it picks is on another day, so set max_time_diff in either function to limit how far away the step may be.

mask() has two rules for the nearest depth level:

  • method = "nearest" (default, as in extract_to_point()) takes the level nearest the detection’s depth, skipping levels without a value.
  • method = "nearest_level" takes the level nearest the detection’s depth even if it has no value, so the detection gets NA there.

"bottom" takes the deepest level with a value and "surface" the shallowest level, as in extract_to_point().

This file has a value at every level, so the next chunk removes the 10 m level from a copy of the voxel. Detection A at 12 m then takes the 0 m level by default, 12 m away, which is nearer than the 25 m level. With "nearest_level" it gets NA. "bottom" takes the 200 m level, the same value extract_to_point() gives:

gappy <- v
gappy[[2]] <- NA_real_   # the 10 m level
summarise_3d(mask(gappy, a), statistic = "mean")
#>         time  mean n
#> 1 2020-03-01 28.35 1
summarise_3d(mask(gappy, a, method = "nearest_level"), statistic = "mean")
#>         time mean n
#> 1 2020-03-01   NA 0
summarise_3d(mask(v, a, method = "bottom"), statistic = "mean")
#>         time  mean n
#> 1 2020-03-01 16.35 1
extract_to_point(obs[1, ], path, var = "temp", date_col = "date",
                 method = "bottom")$temp
#> [1] 16.35

Many points at once

Repeating these steps for thousands of detections reads one window per detection. terra::extract() on the proxy gives the same values for all of them in one call, and takes the same method. It returns one row per detection, with the time step used in time_step and the depth level used in depth_level:

terra::extract(proxy, detections)
#>   feature_id value  time_step depth_level
#> 1          A 27.75 2020-03-01          10
#> 2          B 25.05 2020-03-02          50
#> 3          C 21.95 2020-03-04         100

With bind = TRUE, as in terra, it returns the detections themselves with value, time_step and depth_level added to their columns, ready to keep working with as shapes.

Surface data: a variable without depth

Sea-surface temperature, chlorophyll and many satellite products have no depth. Read them with terra::rast() on the proxy, which gives a plain one-layer raster with the step’s date. The other steps are the same as for a voxel, except that mask() uses only the detection’s position, not its depth, and summarise_3d() weights each cell by its area. Here the surface file holds the top depth level of the example temperature.

sst <- ncdf4::ncvar_def("sst", "degC", dims[c(1, 2, 4)], missval = -9999,
                        prec = "double")
sst_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".nc")
nc <- ncdf4::nc_create(sst_path, sst)
surface <- array(temp, lengths(lapply(dims, `[[`, "vals")))[, , 1, ]
ncdf4::ncvar_put(nc, sst, surface)
ncdf4::nc_close(nc)

sst_proxy <- as_proxy(sst_path)
r <- terra::rast(crop(sst_proxy, a), time = a)[[1]]
summarise_3d(mask(r, a), statistic = "mean")
#>         time  mean n
#> 1 2020-03-01 28.35 1

The result is the surface temperature in the cell of detection A on its day, from one value (n = 1). It is warmer than the 10 m value above, because the example water cools with depth.

Buffers: the water around each detection

buffer_3d() turns each detection into a polygon: here a circle of 5 km radius, from 20 m above to 20 m below the detection, and one day either side.

buffers <- buffer_3d(detections, radius_km = 5, depth_window = 20,
                     time_window = 1)
as.data.frame(buffers)[c("feature_id", "depth_min", "depth_max",
                         "time_start", "time_end")]
#>   feature_id depth_min depth_max time_start   time_end
#> 1          A         0        32 2020-02-29 2020-03-02
#> 2          B        28        68 2020-03-01 2020-03-03
#> 3          C       120       160 2020-03-03 2020-03-05

The steps are the same as for one detection, run for each buffer in turn. as_voxel() returns one voxel for each time step inside a buffer’s window: three for B and C, and two for A, whose window starts before the first day of data. Given that list of voxels, summarise_3d() gives one row per time step. By default the mean is weighted by the volume of water each value stands for, and n counts the values used.

mask() uses only a buffer’s outline and depth range, because as_voxel() has already used its time. It prints a message saying so each time, which suppressMessages() hides inside the loop.

buffer_rows <- lapply(seq_along(buffers), function(i) {
  b <- buffers[i]
  voxels <- as_voxel(crop(proxy, b), time = b)
  inside <- lapply(voxels, function(v) suppressMessages(mask(v, b)))
  rows <- summarise_3d(inside, statistic = c("mean", "sd"))
  cbind(feature_id = as.data.frame(b)$feature_id, rows)
})
do.call(rbind, buffer_rows)
#>   feature_id       time     mean        sd  n
#> 1          A 2020-03-01 27.36252 0.5863953 24
#> 2          A 2020-03-02 27.56252 0.5863953 24
#> 3          B 2020-03-01 25.38426 0.7445443 16
#> 4          B 2020-03-02 25.58426 0.7445443 16
#> 5          B 2020-03-03 25.78426 0.7445443 16
#> 6          C 2020-03-03 18.32145 3.1053138 12
#> 7          C 2020-03-04 18.52145 3.1053138 12
#> 8          C 2020-03-05 18.72145 3.1053138 12

Each row summarises one time step; summarise_3d() doesn’t pool values across steps.

Tracks: buffers along a route

A track is a line with a depth and a time at each vertex. This tag records three positions over 30 hours:

route <- data.frame(
  tag = "D",
  lon = c(150.15, 150.45, 150.85),
  lat = c(-20.85, -20.50, -20.40),
  depth = c(5, 60, 20),
  time = as.POSIXct(c("2020-03-02 00:00", "2020-03-02 12:00",
                      "2020-03-03 06:00"), tz = "UTC")
)
track <- as_vector3d(route, type = "lines", id = "tag", time = "time")

A single buffer around the line would span its full depth and time range, from 5 m to 60 m over two days. To follow the route more closely, sample_3d() places points along it, here at most 10 km apart. Each point gets the depth and time interpolated between the vertices either side, and support_km, the length of route it stands for: half the distance to the points either side.

samples <- sample_3d(track, spacing_km = 10)
as.data.frame(samples)[c("feature_id", "distance_km", "depth", "time",
                         "support_km")]
#>    feature_id distance_km depth                time support_km
#> 1         D_1    0.000000     5 2020-03-02 00:00:00   4.978544
#> 2         D_2    9.957087    16 2020-03-02 02:24:00   9.957087
#> 3         D_3   19.914175    27 2020-03-02 04:48:00   9.957087
#> 4         D_4   29.871262    38 2020-03-02 07:12:00   9.957087
#> 5         D_5   39.828350    49 2020-03-02 09:36:00   9.957087
#> 6         D_6   49.785437    60 2020-03-02 12:00:00   9.296733
#> 7         D_7   58.421816    52 2020-03-02 15:36:00   8.636379
#> 8         D_8   67.058195    44 2020-03-02 19:12:00   8.636379
#> 9         D_9   75.694574    36 2020-03-02 22:48:00   8.636379
#> 10       D_10   84.330953    28 2020-03-03 02:24:00   8.636379
#> 11       D_11   92.967333    20 2020-03-03 06:00:00   4.318190

You then buffer each point and loop over the buffers as above. Here each buffer is a circle of 3 km radius, from 10 m above to 10 m below its point. The loop passes the point, not the buffer, to as_voxel(), which then reads the time step nearest the point’s time. A buffer would need a time window wide enough to contain a step; with daily data and a window of a few hours, as_voxel() stops because the window holds no step. Each row also keeps its point’s support_km, so the weights stay with their rows:

sample_buffers <- buffer_3d(samples, radius_km = 3, depth_window = 10)
local <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(sample_buffers), function(i) {
  b <- sample_buffers[i]
  v <- as_voxel(crop(proxy, b), time = samples[i])[[1]]
  cbind(feature_id = as.data.frame(b)$feature_id,
        support_km = as.data.frame(b)$support_km,
        summarise_3d(suppressMessages(mask(v, b)), statistic = "mean"))
}))
local
#>    feature_id support_km       time     mean n
#> 1         D_1   4.978544 2020-03-02 27.07144 8
#> 2         D_2   9.957087 2020-03-02 26.44616 8
#> 3         D_3   9.957087 2020-03-02 26.64616 8
#> 4         D_4   9.957087 2020-03-02 25.42175 8
#> 5         D_5   9.957087 2020-03-02 25.10001 4
#> 6         D_6   9.296733 2020-03-02 25.20001 4
#> 7         D_7   8.636379 2020-03-03 25.41667 3
#> 8         D_8   8.636379 2020-03-03 26.02175 8
#> 9         D_9   8.636379 2020-03-03 26.02175 8
#> 10       D_10   8.636379 2020-03-03 26.10508 6
#> 11       D_11   4.318190 2020-03-03 27.44616 8

Each row is a local summary: the conditions inside one buffer. n varies from buffer to buffer, here from 3 to 8 values, because the buffers are smaller than the grid cells and the depth window catches one or two levels. A buffer with no water, for example on land near a coast, has a NA mean and n = 0.

To summarise the whole track, average the local means weighted by support_km. This estimates the mean along the distance travelled, from the water the buffers cover, so a stretch of route sampled more densely doesn’t count for more. To weight by time spent instead, use the support_seconds column. na.rm = TRUE leaves out buffers with no water:

stats::weighted.mean(local$mean, local$support_km, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 25.96283

The weights ignore n, so a buffer with 3 values counts as much as one with 8. This is a mean of the local means, not a mean over all the water the buffers cover. These buffers don’t overlap, but neighbouring ones can use the same grid cells, so the local summaries aren’t independent.

sample_3d() doesn’t yet check that each segment stays in water, so check that your samples aren’t on land before summarising them (#105).

Areas: a protected area down to 50 m

An area is a polygon with a depth range. This one covers the middle of the grid, from the surface to 50 m:

mpa <- sf::st_sf(
  name = "reef",
  geometry = sf::st_sfc(sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(
    c(150.3, -20.7), c(150.7, -20.7), c(150.7, -20.3), c(150.3, -20.3),
    c(150.3, -20.7)
  ))), crs = 4326)
)
reef <- as_vector3d(mpa, depth_min = 0, depth_max = 50)
volume(reef) # km³
#> [1] 92.38822

The area has no time, so pick the time step with a date. by = "depth" gives one row per depth level:

v <- as_voxel(crop(proxy, reef), time = "2020-03-03")
summarise_3d(mask(v, reef), statistic = c("mean", "min", "max"),
             by = "depth")
#>         time depth     mean   min   max  n
#> 1 2020-03-03     0 28.40017 28.05 28.75 64
#> 2 2020-03-03    10 27.80017 27.45 28.15 64
#> 3 2020-03-03    25 26.90017 26.55 27.25 64
#> 4 2020-03-03    50 25.40017 25.05 25.75 64
#> 5 2020-03-03   100       NA    NA    NA  0
#> 6 2020-03-03   200       NA    NA    NA  0

The 50 m level counts because the water it stands for, from 37.5 m to 75 m, overlaps the area’s depth range; vignette("depth-levels") describes this rule. The 100 m and 200 m levels are outside the area, so their rows have NA and n = 0.

extract_to_area(mpa, proxy, min_depth = 0, max_depth = 50, time = "2020-03-03") runs the same crop(), as_voxel() and mask() steps in one call, and returns the same voxel.

Down to the seafloor

A depth range that follows the seafloor, such as a species found from the surface down to 200 m or the bed, whichever is shallower, or a layer within 20 m of the bed, varies from cell to cell. vect_to_envelope() builds it on the data’s grid, taking each depth limit as a number or a raster. Here a synthetic bathymetry deepens from 20 m in the west to 320 m in the east. Bathymetry such as GEBCO is elevation, negative below sea level, so flip its sign and set land to 0 before use, then resample it onto the voxel’s grid:

elevation <- terra::rast(nrows = 10, ncols = 10, xmin = 150, xmax = 151,
                         ymin = -21, ymax = -20, crs = "EPSG:4326")
elevation <- -(20 + 300 * (terra::init(elevation, "x") - 150))
seafloor <- terra::resample(terra::clamp(-elevation, lower = 0), v)

to_bed <- vect_to_envelope(mpa, v, depth_min = 0,
                           depth_max = list(200, seafloor))
volume(to_bed) # km³
#> [1] 307.1901
summarise_3d(mask(v, to_bed), statistic = c("mean", "min", "max"))
#>         time     mean   min   max   n
#> 1 2020-03-03 22.04723 16.05 28.75 360

near_bed <- vect_to_envelope(mpa, v, depth_min = list(seafloor - 20),
                             depth_max = seafloor)
summarise_3d(mask(v, near_bed), statistic = c("mean", "min", "max"))
#>         time     mean   min   max  n
#> 1 2020-03-03 18.65017 16.05 22.75 72

In each cell, the deepest depth_min and the shallowest depth_max given apply. Use this instead of as_vector3d() when the range’s top or bottom depends on the seafloor or another surface.

Through time: habitat volume per day

volume() on the proxy measures each time step in turn, in km³. Pass fun to count only some values as habitat, here water between 24 and 26 °C:

volume(proxy, fun = function(x) x >= 24 & x <= 26)
#>         time volume_km3
#> 1 2020-03-01   490.6675
#> 2 2020-03-02   424.1851
#> 3 2020-03-03   357.7448
#> 4 2020-03-04   302.8561
#> 5 2020-03-05   259.5079

The habitat shrinks from day to day because the synthetic water warms each day.

For the habitat inside the area only, keep the habitat in one day’s voxel with occupied(). Masking it by the area would keep whole depth levels, so the 50 m level would count water down to 75 m, below the area’s floor. Instead, turn the habitat into a depth range per cell with voxel_to_envelope() and intersect it with the area, which cuts it at 50 m:

habitat <- occupied(v, function(x) x >= 24 & x <= 26)
inside <- intersect_3d(voxel_to_envelope(habitat), reef)
volume(inside) # km³
#> [1] 23.097

Putting the rows together

The buffer loop ends with a list of data frames, one per buffer, each starting with the buffer’s feature_id. do.call(rbind, ...) joins them into one table, which you can then join back to the observations by ID. In the result, date is the detection date and time is the time step the values come from:

results <- do.call(rbind, buffer_rows)
merge(obs, results, by.x = "tag", by.y = "feature_id")
#>   tag    lon    lat depth       date       time     mean        sd  n
#> 1   A 150.21 -20.31    12 2020-03-01 2020-03-01 27.36252 0.5863953 24
#> 2   A 150.21 -20.31    12 2020-03-01 2020-03-02 27.56252 0.5863953 24
#> 3   B 150.52 -20.56    48 2020-03-02 2020-03-01 25.38426 0.7445443 16
#> 4   B 150.52 -20.56    48 2020-03-02 2020-03-02 25.58426 0.7445443 16
#> 5   B 150.52 -20.56    48 2020-03-02 2020-03-03 25.78426 0.7445443 16
#> 6   C 150.80 -20.82   140 2020-03-04 2020-03-03 18.32145 3.1053138 12
#> 7   C 150.80 -20.82   140 2020-03-04 2020-03-04 18.52145 3.1053138 12
#> 8   C 150.80 -20.82   140 2020-03-04 2020-03-05 18.72145 3.1053138 12
